BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S.O, 62-YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
That this House condemn the tragic implications of monetarist economic policies adopted by this Government that resulted in 24 per cent unemployment among young Canadians and that deny reasonable job prospects for the 300,000 young Canadians graduating from post-secondary institutions this Spring.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise today to open this debate with regard to youth unemployment in the country. That is an ironic statement in light of the tragedy that is facing our youth today. It is absolutely necessary to bring to the attention of the House the plight of our young people and it is crucial that we bring to the attention of the Government the concern that we on this side of the House have for them and their need for jobs. It is important that we bring to the attention of the Government the feelings, the concerns, the hopes and aspirations of young people across the country. That is why we put forward the motion with regard to youth unemployment and that is why we chose to make this the priority of the day for the House.
[DOT]	(mo)
Young people in Canada today, according to Statistics Canada, are unemployed at the rate of 34.4 per cent in the month of March, which means that there are some 650,000 young Canadians out of work. This compares, Mr. Speaker, with an unemployment rate for adults in the country as a whole of 13.9 per cent-that is unadjusted, Mr. Speaker-and some 1,658,000 Canadians out of work, again according to Statistics Canada. These statistics do not take into account the discouraged or underemployed worker. If one compares the
650,000	unemployed young people with the 1,658,000 of the general population who are unemployed, one finds that somewhere between one-third and one-half of unemployed Canadians today are young people between the ages of 15 and 24. Therefore to a very large extent the unemployment problem in this country is a problem of unemployed young people.
Clearly today there are previously unheard of numbers of middle-aged people, heads of households, who are used to steady, well paid employment and are without work. This is, indeed, an unprecedented tragedy which is happening in our country, certainly since the great Depression of the 1930s.
However, a very significant and very important part of the unemployment problem today is the unemployed young people which comprise one-third to one-half of the general population.
One of the reasons it is important to bring this tragedy to the attention of this House today, Mr. Speaker, is the over-all economic policies of the Government of the day and the failure of those economic policies to provide work for Canadians. The young people of Canada suffer much more from unemployment than many of their older brethren due to the policies of this Government as illustrated in its budget, which gives very little hope to people who are unemployed. The Government, by its own actions, by its own economic analyses and its own economic papers, has accepted the extremely high levels of unemployment. It has accepted that for this year there will be some 12.4 per cent unemployed overall. It has accepted that in the medium to long term there will be at least 10 per cent unemployment.
Looking from the perspective of a whole decade, the Government will be seeking to bring down unemployment to something like 7 per cent or 8 per cent, which shows that the Government has really accepted a very harsh view of the world, a view which leaves a very significant proportion of our people unemployed and an even higher level of unemployment among young people. This Government with its policies and actions, therefore, leaves very little hope for the future to young people in the present circumstances.
Young people suffer particularly from unemployment, Mr. Speaker, because, first of all, they lack experience in the job market. When they go to an employer to ask for a job they are told they must have experience, so this lack becomes a barrier to their getting work. This problem is particularly difficult these days because even people who have considerable experience and demonstrated capabilities in a particular occupation are unemployed. Young people also lack training. There is a waiting list for all the training programs in this country. Many people who apply for training under these programs find themselves on those waiting lists. Even many of those people today who are trained and have skills are unemployed, so it is doubly difficult for the young person today to get work because of lack of experience and training in a world where many who have that experience and training are themselves unemployed.
It is particularly important, Mr. Speaker, to pay attention to the plight of young people today because they are forming their first impressions, their views of the working world. Work, Mr. Speaker, should be a satisfying and self-fulfilling activity,

something which gives a person an opportunity to serve the community and grow and learn. But by today's standards young people's impression of the work world and work is just the opposite. They are unable to find work or, when they do, it is insecure and short term. Their experience in the work world is one of frustration.
This is not a good attitude to be fostering in this land. It is important, if a nation is to be strong and its people are to be happy, that work be a satisfying, self-fulfilling activity and that people see work from that perspective. They cannot do it unless they experience it that way, and young people today entering the labour market are experiencing frustration, disillusionment and hopelessness. Young people entering the work world today find they cannot get work, even given their best efforts, and they are unable to deal with this new, harsh reality. They end up with a feeling of powerlessness.
It is important that we take note of that feeling, Mr. Speaker, because in Canada young people form their political ideas, a notion of themselves as an active citizenry, much later than they do in other western democracies such as the United States or Great Britain. The fact that young people coming on to the job market end up frustrated and powerless has great significance for our democracy. In the final analysis democracy depends upon the faith and belief that you can make a difference in your world, that you can have a real impact upon what is happening to you and your community. If the feeling is just the opposite, then their whole approach to democratic decision making is going to be one of apathy rather than one of participation. And it is crucial in a democracy to have an active citizenry.
The tragedy of youth unemployment is not only that they have a lack of income, Mr. Speaker. That is significant and it should be paid attention to by this House, but it also relates to the social sense, the quality of community and political life in this country. Not all young people are on the job market looking for work 12 months of the year. There is a significant number of young people in the training and educational institutes, colleges and universities. In fact, there are probably more people in university today than ever before, because they read the newspapers and see what is happening on the street and they know there are extremely high levels of unemployment. Therefore many have postponed their entering the job market and university enrolment levels have ballooned. We are going to have to keep an eye on this. These people are going to be graduating and when they do, they will need employment. The Government brought down its National Training Act a full year ago and started to train young people for new occupations. A year from now, when those young people start graduating from their community colleges, they are going to need work and if they do not get it they are going to start asking: Why have we trained? They are going to feel double disillusionment and disappointment and alienation.
Seeing no prospect in the budget of employment for these people when their training is up paints a picture of a dismal future, a future about which the Government has chosen not to do anything significant. However, the point I wanted to make about students is that they depend upon employment as well. While they are going to school, there are a number of months in which they are looking for work, and they look for work for a number of reasons. One of the reasons relates to the fact that students pay a significant proportion of their own education costs and, all across the country, tuition fees are rising, at least in part, because of the restraint in transfer payments from the federal Government to provincial Governments. However, tuition fees are rising and the percentage of the cost of education which a student pays is increasing. Therefore, the summer employment of students, the capacity of students to earn and save money for their own education, is very crucial and increasingly important.
However, not only do students seek summer employment to help pay for their own education, they also seek it for the experience of work, for the pleasure of productivity, in order to get out there in the world and find out what the work world is like so they can begin more clearly to define their aspirations for the future, what kind of services they want to provide to the community, what kind of employment they would like to engage in. Therefore, employment for students is crucial in terms of their being able to afford their education and also to learn from their experience.
I would like to say a few words about the student employment programs and youth employment programs of the Government. I have in my hand a copy of "The Budget in Brief'. There is a section dealing with direct employment programs and one dealing with youth programs. Not only have the Government's general economic policies failed to provide employment for youths, but its specific youth employment programs fall far short of the mark as well. They do not reach the target, let alone score a bull's-eye.
I mention these programs rather than just economic policies in general because, even if we had a booming economy, we all know from experience over the last couple of decades that it would still be necessary to have special programs for youth in order to provide them with adequate employment programs.
On page 7 of "The Budget in Brief' of April 19, 1983, under "Youth Programs", there is reference to an additional $70 million which has been allocated for the Summer Canada Program, etc. This would leave one with the impression that on budget night, April 19, 1983, the Government took $70 million out of its pot and put it into the Summer Canada youth programs, $70 million of new money. It refers to "additional dollars". One would have thought that it found the money in the same pot that it found the $200 million to save the reputation of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde).
I have consulted with a number of people including the Canadian Federation of Students. To the best that we can piece the information together, this additional $70 million has been announced at least twice now. Some time in December or
April 26, 1983

January, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) announced some $100 million for Summer Canada youth programs and then some time later, in February or March, raised it to $170 million. The Government now takes that same additional $70 million and announces it again in the budget. Therefore, while the Government was able to find $200 million to save the reputation of the Minister of Finance, or at least to paper it over, it has simply reannounced the additional $70 million.
The additional disappointment about the $70 million is the fact that if one compares the amount which the Government is spending this year on youth programs, $170 million, to the amount that it spent in 1979-and I forget the exact figure but it was around $112 million-one finds that the amount of dollars which the Government is putting into Summer Canada for youth in real terms, taking inflation into account at about 10 per cent, is the same this year as it was in 1979. The real dollar commitment, adjusted for inflation, is at the same level as it was in 1979, even though we are all aware that the economic circumstances are very different from what they were a couple of years ago. As well, the need of young people for employment is much greater this summer than it was a couple of years ago. I point this out specifically because it is important for the Government to have adequate youth programs.
Let me briefly mention the two other announcements made in this document. One concerns Katimavik which provides $40 million for 4,000 participants. I must say that although that is commendable, Katimavik is not really an employment program. It is a program that provides an opportunity to young people to serve their communities. It is not a program which provides a full wage for a full day's work; it is an opportunity for youth to serve their community at below minimum wage. While it is a good program and a worthy idea, I suggest that to list it as direct support for employment is misleading. Once again, while it is a good opportunity it is not an employment program.
The other announcement of direct support for employment which I want to comment on briefly is the one under the Department of National Defence, which provides $75 million over two fiscal years to hire 5,000 young people. Obviously there will be many young people lining up at the Department of National Defence to take advantage of this opportunity because they need work wherever they can find it. Of course, young people will join the Armed Forces, like anyone else, since they want to serve their country and take advantage of this option. The difficulty is that if there are no other real options for young people, they will feel obliged to take this option when they should have choices.
This brings me to another aspect of my concern about youth. The value of youth is the hope that they bring to the country. Therefore it is important for us to provide significant employment for young people, so they can gain experience as well as

pay for their education and ultimately grow and add to the strength of our country.
Youth are not only concerned about themselves. They are concerned about the survival of this planet upon which we live. The youth of today have taken a great deal of initiative to fight the efforts to test the Cruise missile in this country. They tie this issue to employment as well by pointing out that many more jobs can be provided through social spending than military spending.
I see that my time is almost up, but let me say that it is very important for the Government to support the efforts of youth to disarm this world because it is that kind of idealism that will build a better country for the future. Rather than adopting the hawkish attitude of the Government toward the world, we need the hope of youth and should support them in order to make that hope flower.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S.O, 62-YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this because it certainly represents an issue that has been of primary concern to Members of the Government and to me personally as Minister of Employment and Immigration. It is an issue that I believe deserves a fair, open and good exchange of views. However, I would hope that we might avoid the traditionally expected Opposition tendency to wag fingers, lay blame and try to find a culprit or scapegoat by accusing the Government of acting improperly. I think the issue we are examining deserves much better than that.
It is an issue which requires a sensible and common sense approach. It is a problem which has been with us, is with us now and will continue to be with us and it represents one of the most significant, social and economic circumstances that we, as Canadians, face. But we do not face it just by ourselves. I do not know whether Members of the House have had an opportunity just recently to read the front page story in the New York Times. The story described the serious plight of European young people who are faced with this issue. Unemployment has been the subject of a wide number of papers and examinations by Governments around the world.
This phenomenon was born out of the baby boom of the Second World War. Over the past 10 or 12 years we have been watching the enormous acceleration of young people into the labour market. The numbers of young people coming into the job market in this decade has almost doubled that of decades before. We are dealing with very large volumes of young people who want a job and are expecting a job. In any of the traditional occupations, ways of providing employment are no longer there.
At the same time as we have been receiving large numbers of young people in the job market, we have also been experiencing a change in the job market. The questionable pattern of moving toward jobs that require high degrees of

April 26, 1983
Supply
skill, far more training and background and the attempt to come to grips with that particular issue is at the centre, and should be at the centre, of our debate. What we have to recognize is the issue of youth employment. It is not simply a product of the existing recession that we are in; it is an ongoing problem which will represent one of the major issues with which we will have to contend for the rest of this decade.
I would recommend to Hon. Members that they look at the documents I tabled in this House last week during the budget debate entitled "Perspective and Labour Market Policy Framework for the 1980s". I believe it gives an accurate and a good account of the kind of demography and work force which we are looking at and how we as a Parliament will be asked to deal with those issues on a continuing basis.
It is wrong to suggest, as the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper) is trying to suggest, that nothing is being done, that everything is going to hell in a hand basket and that no one cares. 1 want to take this opportunity to describe to Members of the House some of the issues into which we have been entering and as well describe some of the direct areas of progress that we are making in coming to grips with this issue.
First, I would like to say that if Hon. Members want to measure the efforts in which we are engaged by sheer dollar or volume terms, I would point out that in my own Department we spend about $2.5 million a day on the employment and training of young people. In fact, in the 1982-83 fiscal year we spent something like $900 million in a combination of training and employment programs directly targeted at the interests of young people. We provided unemployment and training services to over two million young people this past year alone. In the kind of wide-ranging activities we are able to provide, the largest clientele we serve is under the age of 24. We have been investing in a number of initiatives which I think will provide for a very hopeful future for young people.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James resides, as I do, in the Province of Manitoba. I draw to his attention the announcement that I made last Friday in our own Province. The announcement described that, as a result of the investment under the skills growth fund, we were able to invest in close to 1,000 additional training places in Manitoba alone in high technology areas. This has provided a wide range of new training opportunities in computers, robotics, advanced electronics and heavy machinery that we have developed in Manitoba through that investment by the federal Government's skills growth fund in the distribution of training facilities in northern Manitoba and on Indian reserves. We have taken mobile training vans into the rural areas and we are providing a brand-new training centre in the City of Winnipeg.
If the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James is trying to suggest that we are standing still and are not actively engaged in doing things, I would say that he should probably invest 15 cents to buy a newspaper so that he can learn what is going on in his own area. He will be able to discover that the activity in which we are engaging is providing a very sound and important foundation for economic growth.
I can repeat those examples right across the country. We invested in Holland College in Prince Edward Island to train an additional 90 young people in marine technology. We have just put $4 million into the British Columbia Institute of Technology for a new CAD/CAM program, again providing major training for young people in those areas.
We invested something like $14 million in 17 different community colleges and institutions in the Province of Ontario. This will provide something like several thousand additional training opportunities. I could repeat those examples to demonstrate that we are aware of the necessity of addressing the employment needs of young people, primarily by investing in their future, thereby ensuring that they will have the skills and training to allow them to compete for the new kinds of jobs the decade will bring.
In addition to that, Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to point out the evolution that we have gone through in the development of the youth employment strategy that was announced in last week's budget. Last summer we were very conscious of the increasing problem of youth employment and a need to do something about it. We introduced a number of test programs. For example, we started ten experimental youth job corps programs in ten metropolitan centres across Canada. The job corps idea is to help young people who have been on the sidelines in the job market, those who are disadvantaged or who have been chronically unemployed, get counselling, guidance, work experience and training all at the same place. It will allow them to come out of the disadvantaged category and move into the job market.
We have also introduced a network of specialized youth employment centres across Canada. They will provide special placing and support for young people. We have also introduced a number of trial experiments on a wage-subsidy program through the PED Program. This will allow us to test how we can work with the private sector to provide an incentive for young people to get that first job. We used our opportunities last summer to test some of those new programs and to determine what worked well and what did not.
Following that, Mr. Speaker, in January, 1983 I met with all provincial Ministers of Labour and Manpower and introduced a paper on youth employment. I asked them for their cooperation and co-ordination in our youth strategy. Youth employment represents unquestionably one of the most serious issues facing all Governments. But this problem cannot be solved by one Government acting alone. It has to be a combination of efforts.
I am pleased to report that the provincial Ministers have responded. Since that time we have had a series of senior officials working at how we can co-ordinate the various youth employment training programs across Canada. What became very clear in those discussions last January was the necessity of dealing with a problem that has been endemic in our employment market for the last two decades. Young people face special difficulty in the job market getting that first time job experience. That is the breakthrough they have to make, and it is the major barrier which they have to overcome. Unlike
April 26, 1983

many European countries that have a very well defined transition period between formal schooling and work, Canada does not. It is almost a two-year national apprenticeship program. In Canada we have never adopted that, partly because of our fragmented educational system. But we have never adopted the notion that there has to be a transition period between formal schooling and work so that a young person can get work skills and on-the-job training. That is an idea I put forward that we should grow toward, but how can we make it happen?
I think one of the most important productive results of the budget last Tuesday was that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) provided us with an opportunity to enter into a major new youth employment program, an interim program which will allow us to provide direct subsidies to private business, to small business in particular, to universities, to school boards and to non-profit organizations to hire young persons for on-the-job training, so that they are provided with job experience in the workplace combined with training. The $95 million to launch that program in the first year of operation will provide close to 35,000 young people with that opportunity. I did not hear the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James mention that particular initiative, probably because he knows that it is too good or too effective.
It was based upon the proposals we received from a number of youth organizations asking for the opportunity to break down the barrier. We now have that opportunity. We now have the resources to enter into that new interim youth program. It is my intention as Employment Minister to consult first with private business to gain its views on how it should operate and also to work with young people and youth organizations in its implementation. To carry that forward, we will be holding a national conference in August in Newfoundland on youth employment. We have invited a number of the major youth organizations to join with us in a discussion on how we can mount that major youth strategy.
I think this represents to all of us a major launch forward into a new kind of youth employment posture, one that will be combined with the continuation of the youth job corps system which we have established such as Katimavik, and the additional programs in the Department of National Defence, to supplement that. In the budget the Minister of Finance included $280 million in addition to the other moneys in Departments already going into youth employment. It is additional money to provide young people with that first-time opportunity.
It would be wrong to suggest that nothing is being done. In fact, what we see is a fairly well articulated strategy beginning last summer, moving through the proper steps of consultation and resulting in the budget announcement of a new youth employment strategy on the part of the Government. What we really need now is a full partnership with and participation of other sectors of the economy. We need the assistance of the school boards and provincial Governments. Certainly we need
Supply
the full partnership of labour and business in helping us to mount this new youth employment initiative. It will be our intention to seek that consultation with the idea that it must be a national effort and commitment. It is not something one Government alone should be able to mount. All Canadians must concentrate and devote their attention toward coming to grips with the problems associated with young people. That is really the direction and thrust we are taking in Government to deal with the employment issue.
Also we recognize that we must deal with the other side of the ledger, the people who are still in school. As I pointed out, in that area we will be spending over $1 billion this year in providing new high technology training for close to 275,000 or
300,000	Canadians of whom over 50 per cent are young people. Also this year alone we will be investing $100 million in new training facilities, modernizing equipment and bringing in the new kinds of technology so that young people can be trained in the work of the future.
Also we have started a number of support systems which the Hon. Member mentioned, of summer employment for those who are still in school. The federal Government will be providing direct employment jobs this year for over 70,000 young people. We are hoping that that figure will be matched equally by the efforts of provincial and municipal Governments. If they will make a similar kind of effort, we could be providing double the number of jobs directly by Government.
In addition, we recognize that it is the private sector which must provide the major source of employment for young people. It often disturbs me that the New Democratic Party ignores that fact. It does not pay attention to the potential and capability of the private sector in providing young people with employment. That Party seems somehow to gloss over the necessity of ensuring that private employers play their role. In fact, we launched last week a major information campaign to get private employers to provide jobs for summer students. We will be opening some 400 youth employment centres across Canada which will provide places for employers to post available jobs on the market and opportunities for young people to obtain those jobs. We are not only making an appeal to traditional private sector employers but to people who want work done around their homes or offices. It will require a special effort this summer. The information and advertising campaign is designed to ensure that if they have any kind of job, they should contact one of the 400 youth employment centres, post it on the board and we will get a young person to do the job this summer.
It is my hope that through this debate Hon. Members of the Opposition will offer their services to make this program work and will co-operate in ensuring that activities within their own constituency offices will be directed toward that initiative. Rather than using their time and energies in the pursuit of criticism, hopefully they will turn them to somewhat more constructive pursuits during these very critical summer months. I know the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES

Hnatyshyn) will be a major and active supporter of the program. I can see that he has already acknowledged it and given us his support. We will mark his name on the list.
These are the kinds of efforts we are attempting to provide, but I want to return to one fundamental issue. We must recognize that during this period there are no quick-fix solutions. In fact, it was interesting that the opening speaker for the New Democratic Party did not make any offers as to what he would do. He did not have any sort of magic solutions to the problem; he simply criticized what was being done. I think the issue requires much more than that. It will require the best of our creative abilities and energy as Parliamentarians to address this issue, to use our resources effectively and to provide for a better partnership among all major players in the economy.
What the economists call the structural problem of youth employment will be a continuing problem. We must work away at it. We must develop better techniques for bringing people into the labour market. We must make better use of our teaching and training institutions. We must go into the schools and try to give better guidance and information to young people so that they will choose careers which will lead to jobs.
When I talk to young people in the high schools in my constituency, it disturbs me greatly that many of them are preparing themselves in grades eight, nine and ten for jobs which will not be there four or five years from now. The basic information about the changing nature of the job world is not being transmitted or passed into their hands. In passing I want to say that we are trying to address that issue through the implementation of our new Canadian Occupational Projection System. We are trying to provide a much better navigational system for the job market by being able to predict and forecast where future job markets will be. We can obtain that information and give it to guidance counsellors in the schools, to teachers, parents and young people, so that they can begin preparing themselves for careers which will be real ones.
When we go into the schools and talk to young women in the system, they say that they are going to be clerks, stenographers or work in offices. We have to tell them that in four or five years maybe 40 per cent or 50 per cent of that work will be eliminated. They say that no one told them. This simply points out the necessity of working on all fronts with educators to ensure that the basic training and education they offer is relevant and contemporary to labour market needs and to ensure that young people have access to that information.
I am simply suggesting that the issue of youth employment cannot be solved by the wave of a magic wand. It will require a very major combined effort on the part of all sectors of our economy. I hope this debate will help generate that kind of interest, involvement and particularly that kind of co-operation, so that we can address what I consider to be the number one national priority.

Mr. Speaker, the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) is clearly aware that the NDP has long been calling for a serious industrial strategy in the country to
create long-term employment for everyone who wants to work. In terms of immediate action, we have called for significant action on public works and a decent tax break for low and moderate income people to stimulate consumer demand.
I direct a question to the Minister. He talked about economists and structural unemployment among youth. This echoes the Minister of Finance's general statements about structural unemployment for the general population and leads into an acceptance of an extraordinarily high level of unemployment for the general population and for youth. Given the Minister's long list of activities that the Government is involved in and the fact that today there is an unemployment rate among youth of 23.4 per cent, and given his stated concern for students this summer, will he tell this House what level of youth unemployment he expects this summer during the months of June and July? Does he expect that his programs will have a significant impact on the unemployment rate among youth? What are his expectations in terms of their impact on the social reality of this country?

Slippery? I think it is wonderful that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James has now accepted the kind of strategy that we have put forward.
As for his question about statistics, I note how the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James has shifted his ground. He wants to talk about statistics now. We have tried to put forward a strategy that clearly enunciates the method that we believe will succeed in dealing with this problem by working with the private sector in developing a wage subsidy program for on-the-job training so that we can overcome the barrier that young people face, and by using the job corps program as a way of giving chronically unemployed young people the kind of support that they need. We are looking for the same endorsement of those kinds of programs that the Hon. Member just gave to the general budget. We are looking for a willingness to go back and persuade provincial Governments, municipal Governments, the private sector and labour to co-operate so that we can create a national coalition.

Mr. Speaker, because Members of the Opposition love to get hung up on statistical somersaults, I want to point out a statistical phenomenon that exists: the more jobs you create, the more people you are bringing back to the job market; therefore, the indicators do not change but more jobs are being provided. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would ask the Minister a question along the general philosophical line of what is seen in the future for work in general but particularly work for young people. I know the Minister is aware that the problem that exists in Canada is a very real one that is not going to go away instantly, and as he said, there is no magic wand that will take it away. However, one must look at the Canadian situation in relation to the whole world, particularly in relation to countries in Latin America where the majority of the population is young. The world population is growing at the greatest rate in the youth sector and any future planetary economy will be based on all the people in the world working somewhere.
I would ask the Minister if he has in his Department any sort of futuristic planners who are looking at what will happen to Canada in its relationship with the whole world as this massive number of young people come on to the labour markets of this planet. Does he have a futuristic group that will plan for other ways to look upon work in Canada? This may sound a little bit funny, but will it always be necessary for one to have a job to get an income as many of the traditional jobs that provided income in the past disappear? What group or groups will do the creative thinking for the future which, to my mind, will differ from even the recent past?

That is why we are investing so many of our resources in a new training system across Canada, a program that is central to our strategy.
Mr. Speaker, in relation to the Hon. Member's larger question about what we are doing in the world, I do not know

An officer from my Department is in El Salvador at the present time negotiating a specific program for the training of young El Salvadorans in Canada so they can take those skills back to their own country.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S.O, 62-YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to enter the debate today as it is an important one. The whole issue of youth concerns all of us.

April 26. 1983
Supply
I was interested in the Minister's remarks. He started out by saying that we should not point to the sins of the Government. Why is that? Certainly the Government has to take responsibility for some of its actions that have contributed to youth unemployment in the country. The Minister spent a great deal of time talking about Government spending, Government programs and how they would solve all sorts of problems; then he talked about the need for the private sector to create the jobs. I believe that is only lip service, Mr. Speaker. There are some Government programs but the question remains about what they will do for the private sector.
The National Energy Program took away literally thousands of jobs in the country but that matter was not addressed in the budget. Those jobs will not be back on the market this year. There were no changes to the tax regime that would stimulate and encourage the private sector and small business.
What I think is most significant about the budget is the fact that there is a great deal of talk about helping the private sector. We were hoping for some recovery this year but next year new taxes will come in that may stifle any revitalization of the economy that could take place in 1983.
The Minister talked about creating 600,000 new jobs. As my colleague from St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) stated, we find that 500,000 young people will be out looking for their first full-time job this year. They may get some of those jobs. The problem is serious when the Minister admits that unemployment is going to continue well into 1986 when we will still have an unemployment rate hovering around 10 per cent. That means youth unemployment will still be very high.
The problems that face all young people in Canada are staggering. At the moment we have 658,000 unemployed young Canadians, or 23.4 per cent. One out of every four young people in Canada is presently without a job. When we start to break the figures down we find that of the 2 million who are employed, roughly 700,000 are only employed parttime. Half the people who are employed part-time are looking for full-time jobs although they are not registered as unemployed. That brings in another 300,000 young people. They have a difficult time of it because they have no job security. Virtually always they receive low wages. I could give examples of businesses which keep people on part-time employment because they can pay them lower wages. Thus, they receive a sketchy training and have little opportunity in the future. The underemployed have a difficult time of it today.
The figures do not even consider what we call the "uncounted", the discouraged people who have quit looking for work and those who are making a tawdry living at best on the streets-the hidden unemployed. These young people are developing the worst possible attitude toward their future. They feel there is no future for them, and they have no pride because there is nothing they can do.
So, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak to the motion. The people we are talking about, the young people, are the last to be hired and the first to be fired. They certainly need our attention and consideration and they need to see a demonstration of our concern.
I am glad that the motion we are addressing includes consideration of the situation of this year's graduates and what
they are going to face. Looking through some figures taken from various engineers' associations I find that since 1981 unemployment among engineers has risen by 500 per cent. This spring 7,000 graduates will be looking for new employment opportunities, and unemployment in the engineering field is already up by 500 per cent. Many of the graduates from last year have not found jobs, yet this new group is coming onstream. They will have little opportunity for employment.
When the Hon. Member drafted his motion he perhaps cast his net a little too narrowly. It is not monetarism alone that is responsible for the situation. There is a need for the Government to try and curb Government caused inflation. Its deficits, its intervention and its fiscal irresponsibility are among the root causes of youth and general unemployment in the country. In 1973 the gross debt was about $46 billion; we understand that today it is around $160 billion. That is certainly a significant increase, Mr. Speaker.
The Government does not seem inclined to do anything about its wasteful habits. It has looked around for someone to take the blame and has hit on the Bank of Canada. The Government chose not to do the necessary hard work itself. It did not stop the advocacy advertising that we have just seen on the Crow rate. That is the kind of thing that needs a great deal of money, just to bring the viewpoint of the Government to the public. It is a viewpoint that has not been discussed in Parliament and certainly is not reflected in legislation. It is what I call propaganda and is a considerable waste of Government funds. The Government has not watched the spending of Crown corporations and some examples of this have caused concern. A recent television program on Canadair's Challenger executive jet showed that it involved a cost of over $1.5 billion. Some jobs were created but Parliament still has to see a review of Canadair operations and has not had a chance to discuss the implications of the Government funds going into it.
Consolidated Computer has cost $125 million over the past ten years. That money has gone, Mr. Speaker; it is wasted. It could have been used to create jobs or as an incentive in the private sector, but instead it may well have contributed to inflation.
I am concerned that the motion does not really understand the impact of the broad range of Government policies. I mentioned the plight of engineering graduates. One of the major employers of engineers is the oil and gas industry. It used to employ a lot of engineering skills but neither that industry nor related industries have had a great need for engineers lately. That all came about as a result of the national energy policy. Two years ago I was in Calgary talking to employers of engineers and asking what opportunities were available to young engineers coming out of our universities. Formerly, those young people were able to go into head offices and negotiate a job as though they had five, 10 or 15 years' experience, the demand for their services was so strong. It is not there today. Since the National Energy Program was brought in those graduates have been looking for work.
April 26, 1983

The Minister from Quebec shakes his head, but I live in that area and I happen to know that people employed in that sector are no longer employed and no longer have that opportunity. That is true of those in related industries. There are a lot of industries which are related and are spin-offs from the energy sector. You do not see the growth that occurred in the towns and cities which once were booming and creating employment opportunities, not just for Albertans but for people right across the country. In my own riding there were people from Quebec, Ontario and virtually every Province in Canada who were employed. Today they do not have those jobs or that opportunity because of things like the National Energy Program.
We still import some 250,000 barrels of oil a day. The National Energy Program prices our petroleum products right out of the international market. We know those concerns are there because of the problems we are facing with natural gas exports. That programs which is demonstrative of what we could be encouraging in the private sector, is a real example of what is not being done. It is a contributor to our youth unemployment, not just for the engineers, as I mentioned, but for construction personnel. Anyone who knows anything about the energy sector knows that these projects which we have been talking about require literally thousands and thousands of people to work on them, from the unskilled to the most highly skilled. But that is not happening. There is no construction personnel. There are no "roughnecks" any more. In my area there used to be as many as 65 or 70 rigs going all the time, all of which employed young men and women. Today they are down to five, 10, 15. The jobs are gone.
What causes me some real concern is a new attitude which I sense is coming. I was very interested in the question which was just put to the Minister, and that is, where are we going in the future? What is the significance? What is happening? What causes me concern is this solution of work sharing, this idea of work sharing. Because we are not going to be able to provide employment for our young people in Canada on an ongoing basis, we are going to have them share jobs. I find that very offensive.
I come from a part of the country which is rich in resources, whether it be oil or gas, or the sands which can be turned into glass. There is the kind of opportunity in this country which is hard for us to imagine. People from other countries look at us and say: "My goodness, you have everything". We have everything and we still have a very small population. The question is, then, if we have all those opportunities and resources, why are our young people unemployed? I believe it has to be very clearly because of the fact that the Government has not provided any stimulus or incentive to see those resources brought onstream in order to create and provide opportunities for young people right across Canada.
Another concern, and I suppose this is the one most often referred to, is that of interest rates. I believe that interest rates over the last couple of years have had an impact on bankruptcies. In 1982 we had some 90 per cent more bankruptcies than in 1979. In 1982 there were some 10,700, close to 11,000
Supply
bankruptcies. In 1983 we find that we already have about 2,800 bankruptcies in the first three months of this year.
That is a very serious problem because those businesses, those private sector small businesses which are going bankrupt, are not doing business, are not hiring and are not creating jobs for young Canadians. There is now a modest reprieve from the high interest rates of last year and the year before, but the question still remains, what is coming next? The Government has just told us in this last budget that we are going to be looking at deficits of over $20 billion for the next decade. That is obviously going to put pressure on the market and on interest rates, and it has to. The Hon. Member opposite should know that. When interest rates climb, business opportunities in this country and employment opportunities for our young Canadians must be affected.
The great concern, however, is that of youth unemployment. I believe that the Government is responsible for this problem in a number of ways. The problems our young people are facing are massive. We have over 600,000 unemployed, we have over
300,000	underemployed, we have approximately 600,000 seeking summer jobs, and we have over 500,000 who will be seeking their first full-time job this year. If we total up those figures we will find that it has significant impact and is a problem of very serious magnitude.
It is no wonder that these young people have high levels of frustration and very little sense of hope or sense of where they can go in the future. But what is the Government doing about it? Something that really stunned me when I heard the Minister refer to it was the study called "Perspective on employment: A Labour Market Policy Framework for the 1980s". This report indicates that Government is redefining acceptable unemployment levels. My understanding is that it is now going to accept 8 per cent instead of 3 per cent. That is an acceptable level of unemployment in a country like Canada? That is an acceptable level of unemployment in a country of opportunity and potential? Right now we have unemployment running at 12 per cent to 12.5 per cent and we can virtually double that figure for our youth who are running at 24 per cent. Does that mean that if we have an acceptable level of unemployment in this country of 8 per cent across the board, then it is acceptable to have 16 per cent unemployment among our young people in this country? I find that, Mr. Speaker, very unacceptable. I feel that is something which is very serious and we should be looking at it, because historically our youth has had a hard time finding employment. Youth unemployment has always been high. Does this new definition mean that unemployment among the young is to be acceptable at 16 per cent or 18 per cent?
The Government has indicated it is making work for the young people of Canada. We just heard the Minister recite a number of programs which are coming forward. I applaud him for those programs, but in reality is the Government really doing very much? Take, for example, the youth internship and wage subsidies for the young, a program worth $95 million. If you break that down for the 500,000 young people who are seeking their first full-time job this year, it works out to about
24850

April 26, 1983
Supply
$190 per person. If we give them some sort of a wage subsidy of $2 or $3, what kind of an impact is that going to have? That amount of subsidy per person would hardly last more than a couple of weeks. So we must get this problem into perspective and realize just how serious it is and how much of a pittance that $95 million really becomes when you are talking about literally millions of young Canadians.
The Government has indicated it cannot spend very much more money; it cannot continue to spend more money than it has. The problem is that it spent the money when the economy did not need it. Now when we are in a situation where we desperately need some funding and some help, the money is not there because it was wasted in the past. We get lip service now that the private sector is going to be helped and encouraged, that the Government is going to do this and do that. I do not believe very much is going to happen.
I would like to conclude by saying that I believe this whole situation of youth and general unemployment is partly a result of this Government's cavalier attitude towards the private sector and of its massive and costly intrusion into the very private lives of Canadians. I believe the National Energy Program is probably one of the most prime examples of that. It is a program which could have been creating jobs in a sector which was alive and well and which had lots of potential, but which has now ground to a halt. We are left with a Minister who has to stand and list off Government programs, and we know that even if youth took every job which the Minister has just indicated will be created, it would barely employ those people who are taking their first full-time job this season. It is a serious problem, Mr. Speaker, and it will take an awful lot more incentive from this Government to create the very real jobs which are needed by the young people of Canada.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S.O, 62-YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to the comments of the previous speaker, the Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper). After listening to him in English and then using my earphone to find out whether it sounded better in French, I realized that the Hon. Member used his entire twenty minutes to make a post mortem of the past recession. I sincerely believed there was a new generation of Members in the Progressive Conservative Party. When the Hon. Member rose, I felt that here was one of the younger elements of the Progressive Conservative Party who would use his imagination and avoid the usual cliches in criticizing inflation, which is going to be 6.3 per cent, and the deficit, as he has done. But then he said: Do more and spend less. That does not sound very sensible. He said: The
Government is not doing enough, but he also said: No Government interference! Finally, he treated us to some weeping and gnashing of teeth about the energy problem in Canada, and he was very sorry to see that no large projects were being undertaken. I agree, but the Hon. Member should not blame everything on the National Energy Program. He should realize that oil prices have varied substantially since these projects were developed, and that to be financially viable, many of these projects depended on oil price levels of around $42, and are therefore entirely unrealistic today.
I think all Canadians are going to be disappointed in the speech by the youth critic of the Progressive Conservative Party, because for twenty minutes, he failed to offer any solutions at all. I think he is treading the same path as the leadership candidates. They have absolutely no recommendations to make, and the best they can do is to launch vicious attacks as they do on the leadership candidates in their own party, and I think that I heard the Hon. Member say that we might steal them. If they have any to steal, we would try and implement them, but they have nothing to steal, they have no ideas and I think this is very unfortunate, because the youth problem is one that requires serious study by both Opposition and Government Members.
Earlier, the New Democratic Party made some entirely meaningless comments. The same applies to the Progressive Conservatives. Fortunately, at least our Government Members are being imaginative and looking at programs that can deal with the concerns of young people. Of course, we would all like to have programs that would provide employment for 600,000 young Canadians, but that is impossible in the present situation.
I thought it was very interesting that just a few days after the budget, the New Democratic Party should ask for a debate on youth employment, because it is a subject that is worthy of the undivided attention of all the Members of this House. Unfortunately, I now realize that Hon. Members are more interested in making political points than in offering young Canadians any hope or solutions or jobs.
In fact, the Lalonde Budget has offered a great deal of hope to many people of my generation, if I may say so. In all parts of the country, the budget was received with great satisfaction by businessmen, who saw these programs and fiscal measures as the road to accelerated recovery, and in fact, according to the comments I heard during the last two weekends in my riding they were ready to start new projects and felt that economic recovery was imminent.
I know that, unfortunately in many cases employers will first have to call back employees on the lay-off list before recruiting people from outside, and that is why I welcome these temporary programs. People argue that these are not permanent solutions and are a bandaid approach to the present situation. Actually, I think the Government should not get involved in permanent job creation programs and that its role should be to provide relief in situations like the present one
April 26, 1983

where it will be several months before private enterprise will be able to start hiring young people.
On the other hand, Hon. Members know perfectly well that this summer-in a few weeks-hundreds of thousands of students throughout their ridings are going to start working on projects they themselves proposed. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has set aside $170 million for the Summer Canada program, and when I hear the Members opposite say that we are doing nothing, I would like to point out that they are all delighted to announce these summer jobs in their ridings. I certainly am. Thirty-two projects will start in the riding of Shefford to provide students with interesting work during the summer. That is one of the many programs we are offering. Thanks to the Summer Canada program, and the funding it is able to provide, many young people will be able to pay for their education next year and at the same time acquire some useful experience on the labour market. I think this is an admirable initiative on the part of the Government. There are also summer programs in the Federal public service under which thousands of students will be able to acquire practical experience, and although these programs may not be attractive to everyone, anyone may apply, and applicants who are chosen will be able to work under these programs during the summer.
The Government also has other programs which I intend to discuss in greater detail later on, and these include the NEED program, community development, manpower training, worksharing, National Defence projects and the Katimavik program of the Department of the Secretary of State. At this point I would like to point out that this summer again, the main employer of young people in Canada will, of course, be the private sector.
In this connection, a national advertising campaign, urging the private sector, including industry, businessmen and even private citizens to hire a student this summer, has been launched by Employment and Immigration, under a very striking slogan: Profitez de l'energie scolaire. Embauchez un etudiant cet ete. Earlier, 1 heard the Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper) say that we should not spend money on advertising. I beg to differ. This publicity campaign will help make potential employers aware of the services offered by student employment centres, and as a result, think about having certain jobs done by students. As Hon. Members will see in their own ridings, student employment centres are playing a very significant role throughout Canada.
I would therefore like to take advantage of this opportunity to ask Canadian employers to hire as many young people as they can this summer, either on their own or by asking the Canada Employment Centre or the Student Employment Centre to get the young workers they need.
Incidentally, we are trying to direct young people to entrepreneurs who are able to offer career-oriented job experience. In the past, we have seen that in many cases, such jobs have finally led to permanent employment. In fact, I would say that student employment centres are another important source of
Supply
employment and experience for thousands of our young people, because these centres are, in fact, run by students.
In addition, one sometimes forgets the significant role played by the employment and counselling services of Employment and Immigration Canada. Are Hon. Members aware that, before the June 19 budget last year, the employment strategy for 1983-84 was expected to provide assistance to 2.2 million young Canadians thanks to a $145 million appropriation to Canada Employment and Youth Employment Centers. Are they aware that, in the area of job training, under the Act passed by Parliament last year, $589 million out of a total of over $1 billion allotted this year are to be spent directly for young Canadians and should provide assistance to 140,000 of them? Job-creation programs such as the CCDP, NEED, Katimavik and Summer Canada were allotted $338 million and will provide employment for 107,000 young people. Including the additional $70 million allotted to Summer Canada, which represent 24,000 jobs, the $18 million allotted to the youth-oriented element of the ACCESS Program, which will provide 9,500 jobs, as well as the $2 million granted to the Department of National Defence, which will provide employment for over 4,000 young people, and the additional $10 million provided to Katimavik, which will help another 1,000 young people, the recent federal budget provides an additional $160 million to create 38,000 more jobs for young Canadians. In view of the present economic conditions, Mr. Speaker, this allocation of funds indicates that the Government recognizes the unemployment problem among young people and is willing to spend a lot of money to alleviate it, since it intends to add $160 million to its existing programs and make a special effort to provide assistance during these difficult times.
I might add that the youth employment strategy proposed by the Canadian Government depends on the cooperation and the participation of the young people themselves, as well as of business, labour, and the Provincial and Federal Governments. Speaking of Provincial Governments, I would like to take this opportunity to deal with the NEED Program as it applies to municipalities in Quebec since the PQ Government has refused to cooperate with the Federal Government. We all know that the PQ Government reversed its decision at a time when we had already received from Quebec over 400 municipal projects which could have provided many jobs for young people. Moreover, last week, in my own region, the Minister of Municipal Affairs announced a subsidy program, and what is more, he made something of an overbidding by saying that the Provincial Government would in any cases spend $50 million, while providing a bit more for winter works, and so on. What he did not say publicly, but revealed privately was that all municipalities with employees subject to recall will have to rehire all of them before being eligible for the subsidy program. In other words, the city of Granby, for instance, which

April 26, 1983
Supply
would have received thousands of dollars under the NEED Program if it had been approved for municipalities has 32 employees subject to recall, which means that it would have to rehire these 32 people to be eligible for the provincial subsidy program.
No municipality should consider this as a subsidy because all major cities in Quebec, such as Sherbrooke, Montreal and Quebec, have unionized employees that are subject to recall. This program is therefore nothing but a smokescreen. In my opinion, the Provincial Government is simply seeking wide publicity. However, young people in Granby will not be able to take part in municipal projects because none can be undertaken in the present circumstances.
To come back to youth employment and the Federal programs in this area, I said earlier that the contribution made by the private sector is its most important element. I was therefore glad to see that the NEED Program now provides an opening for the private sector. I would like to give an example of a project which was accepted in my constituency, namely the case of the Ezeflow company which has now decided to upgrade its plant and to relocate. When the NEED program was announced, the owner told me that thanks to the $120,000 grant, he would hire 15 temporary workers for a few weeks, and then he would have to hire 30 permanent workers after moving to the new plant. And if among the 15 employees hired through the NEED Program I find good workers, I will keep them. Consequently, the NEED Program in the private sector may turn out to be a program which will promote the creation of permanent jobs. That is one example among many others which I can now witness in my riding, and I am convinced that everywhere else in the province and throughout the country they have a similar experience. A Member opposite was trying to say earlier that there is too much Government intervention, but all the potential employers whom I met and to whom I mentioned the NEED Program are very anxious to participate in these economic recovery projects, and I am confident indeed that they will create not only temporary jobs for many young Canadians, but permanent jobs as well.
Last week the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) announced that twelve programs will be combined into four. I must admit that I welcome that initiative. Our colleagues opposite may not want to advertise so that people do not get to know our programs, but I for one feel that we do need a bit of publicity and that our programs ought to be as simple as possible to enable Canadians to derive real benefits from them without having to make 32 phone calls, arrange 43 appointments and write letters with umpteen copies. We all know that simplification is the order of the day in a crisis such as we have. Since the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) is in the House, I take this opportunity to commend him for the way he has launched the special projects. He has decided to shorten delays, to do away with bureaucratic red tape, and to get on with the job immediately. In my opinion, the Minister of Employment and Immigration is taking similar action through the NEED Program, the CLE
Program, the ACCESS Program and the Summer Job Corps Program. The twelve federal programs will become four generously funded programs which will be easy to administer and which the interested groups will readily understand. That is why when I hear our colleagues opposite claim that indeed they are concerned about the youth unemployment issue, I am tempted to point out to them, particularly to the Progressive Conservatives, that the last time they raised the question of youth problems in the House was during the Tory convention when the young pro-Clark delegates were given expense accounts to come to Ottawa and fill up the galleries. As I recall, Mr. Speaker, that was the only time the Progressive Conservative Members devoted an oral questions period to the problems of young Canadians, the only time in their history, and it was nothing but a real show.
I am sure that even today they pay lip service to the issue without suggesting a solution because, ever since that convention, they have not given a thought to young people and right now they are less concerned about idle youths than they are about 13 or 14 year old youngsters who are still attending school and whom they want to parade on the convention floor. I hope that once and for all they will come to grips with the problems of young people, not only when they have their leadership brawls. That is the only time we see them.
I conclude my remarks by expressing the hope that within the next few weeks or months Members from both sides of the House will get together in parliamentary committees to examine the overall situation of young people in Canada with respect to unemployment and social issues. I hope as well that the Progressive Conservative Party and the New Democratic Party will select Members who have a little bit of imagination, who will not look upon youngsters as so many more votes at the convention, and who will come up with ideas and solutions. The Government is now working alone, but I would suggest that the problem is so serious that everybody must come to grips with it. Mr. Speaker, I thank you for being so patient and so attentive.

April 26, 1983

Quebec regulations, it became impossible to hire people who otherwise would have been unemployed. The provincial regulations required higher wages than those we had expected to pay. subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S.O, 62-YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on this New Democratic Party Opposition Day to join with Members of the NDP in condemning the Government on behalf of the youth of this country. You will note that the NDP has framed its motion to restrict criticism to condemning the tragic implications of the monetarist policies adopted by the Liberal Government. You will note from my comments, Mr. Speaker, that I will go well beyond restricting criticism to the monetarist policies. In fact, I will condemn the economic, social and fiscal policies of this Government.
I agree the Government has clearly botched the governing of this country. Let us look at the basics. Canada has a small population and we have tremendous resources over which, by the grace of God, we have stewardship. One must then look at the way in which the Government over the last 15 years has botched its stewardship of governing. It has not put in place policies which ensure that our small populace have work and satisfying careers.
I agree with the NDP that the Government has clearly botched its job. The Government has lost touch with reality. It has lost touch with the economic reality of Canada in global terms. It has so concentrated its efforts on internal conflicts, whether with the Government of Quebec, the Government of Alberta, or within the social classes of our country, and on its view of centralizing power, that the Government has forgotten that the primary role we have in this House is to deal with international affairs. If it were not for the Progressive Conservative Party and the New Democratic Party allocating Opposition Days to discuss international affairs, the subject would never be discussed. Yet if you look at our Constitution, our prime responsibility is to deal with international affairs, international trade and defence matters. We never talk about them.
If we were to concentrate on what Canada should be doing in the world, this small population of 24 million people should be working flat out. No doubt people all over the world need our resources. They need to have the benefit of our many many generations of political stability, economic development and general maturity. Canada should be providing capital to the world. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, the capital which 24 million Japanese would generate from the resources we have? Can you imagine the capital that 24 million Germans would generate? Canada would then be a source of wealth to the world. But instead, what are we doing? We are begging on our knees for money from Germany, Japan the the United States. By having to borrow that money we are competing against Third World countries, which in turn drives up interest rates. We are hurting that Third World countries far more than we need to. It is the same with energy. We are competing with Third World countries for energy. Canada should be a source of energy.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) gets a lot of praise in some branches of the media for his high international reputation. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the people to whom I
April 26, 1983

talk internationally do not think our Prime Minister has done a good job; nor do they think that Canada is pulling its weight in the world in terms of defence, in terms of international energy or in terms of international capital flows. Canada has vast resources. We should not be out competing in the world; we should be providing skills to the world, not taking them away.
My point of departure with the NDP motion is that it puts total blame on the Government's abuse of monetary policy. I believe the Government has abused not only monetary policy but social policy, fiscal policy and economic policy. When a Government year after year after year piles on deficits, which is just another way of saying that the Government offers programs to people without a corresponding tax to pay for them, it defers payment to another generation. It is a mortgage on the future. When a Government does that year after year after year, it leads directly to inflation, which we have had; it leads directly to high interest rates, which we have had; and high interest rates lead directly to loss of jobs and bankruptcies, which we have had. Then we have an enormous period of adjustment that is so difficult. The Government has thus violated social policy.
Let me talk about those people who have retired. During all of those years they worked faithfully at their careers and put a little money aside for their pension. But when they were faced with 20 per cent inflation, the value of their pension dropped to half within four or five years. Therefore all our seniors are upset. Those same deficits led to people taking money out of the country rather than investing it here. That procedure has affected our youth because there is a direct correlation between investment of the capital of the nation and jobs. Resources do not mean anything if they are not used.
Let me cite one example. For hundreds of thousands of years, coal lay under the great western plains unused. The native people at the time had a different culture. They walked over it. They had social taboos against using the coal that stuck out of the banks in my own City of Lethbridge, Alberta. It was only when that resource was developed and used that it became wealth, which was redistributed to all parts of our society and generally raised our well-being.
Forests are worth nothing if the trees are left standing. The forests are of value only when the lumber is used. If I take a tree and cut it up, I can sell the lumber somewhere within or outside the country to build furniture, to build houses or factories. If I, as an individual, find oil, I realize that I can build a refinery and turn the oil into propane, butane, gasoline, kerosene and asphalt. But only by people having ideas and acting upon them does oil or other resource take on value.
Peter Pond found the Alberta tar sands 200 or 300 years ago. Yet the Alberta tar sands were nothing until a company, a collection of individuals, decided to put up a syncrude plant, process the oil by running it through hot water, skimming the
oil off the top and then selling it. Only then did that resource take on value and increase our standard of living.
The Government, having driven away all that capital, has taken away jobs. This affects our youth and is why we have youth unemployment of 24 per cent.
All of these ad hoc programs that just keep people occupied for a few weeks at most do not direct themselves to the underlying problem, which is real jobs, not ad hoc jobs. Interestingly enough, the poor parts of the country become poorer and poorer under these ad hoc programs. Let us have a unified effort and develop this country, because the resources are here.
May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF NURSING HOME WITHIN RESIDENCE FOR SENIOR CITIZENS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at a recent official opening of a nursing home for senior citizens in the Hamilton region, I was most favourably impressed with an innovation whereby a 32-bed nursing home
was constructed within a 110-unit senior citizens residence. This was a very progressive step in which the continued need for nursing beds for senior citizens was met.
The details of the financing of this project were under the supervision of Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, but it required a co-operative effort between the federal Government and Ontario provincial authorities to overcome the regulatory restrictions to make the project feasible.
The principal advantage of integrating a nursing home with a senior citizens residence is the reunification of elderly couples, one of whom requires nursing care, and the other, residential facilities. It also brings together medical and paramedical personnel available for the care of senior citizens in both wings of the building project.
My concern is the bureaucratic nightmare that presents itself to non-profit organizations in many areas of the country where similar projects are needed and could replace separate nursing homes and senior residences which currently preclude companionship and closeness of aging couples. Hopefully the results achieved at the Heritage Green senior citizens residence and nursing home in Stoney Creek, Ontario, which combines these two types of facilities, can be duplicated in other parts of the country through federal-provincial cooperation.

subtopic: PROPOSED UNITED STATES RESTRICTIONS ON IMPORTATION OF CANADIAN SCALLOPS
PROPOSED UNITED STATES RESTRICTIONS ON IMPORTATION OF CANADIAN SCALLOPS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Canadian scallop fishing industry is in deep trouble. At the present time the count for scallops exported from Canada to the United States is 40 meats to the pound. On this basis the scallop fishery alone was worth $88 million last year to Canada. About 75 per cent of the 15,000 metric tonnes of scallops caught off the Atlantic Coast last year was exported to our friends south of the border. This market will be devastated if the United States follows through with its proposals to limit scallop imports to 30 meats to the pound on May 15.
The Americans have stated that the proposal to restrict scallop imports to the larger size is being implemented as a conservation measure. Yet when Canadians some three or four years ago requested the American scallop fishing industry to cut down on the number of pounds landed per trip from Georges Bank, they not only continued to overfish the Bank but the American fleet has more than doubled in size.
If the proposal to limit imports of scallops from Canada to 30 meats per pound is implemented by the United States, it will mean that Canada will no longer have a viable scallop fishery. I submit that the American proposal is a non-tariff barrier to trade. This is a fundamental basic resource industry, and I urge the Government to take this matter up with the Americans at the highest possible level.
April 26, 1983

subtopic: DEFENCE INDUSTRY-PARTICIPATION IN UNITED STATES MILITARY PRODUCTION
DEFENCE INDUSTRY-PARTICIPATION IN UNITED STATES MILITARY PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last week it was revealed that the Pentagon is planning to exclude Canada from access to U.S. defence industry development programs partially because Canada has been taking a free ride at U.S. expense, and, more significantly, because they feel our participation would result in the leakage of American secrets to the Soviet Union. The Government's refusal to prosecute Hugh Hambleton and the recent revelations concerning Long Knife, an ex-RCMP officer's betrayal of a Soviet source, serve to reinforce this opinion.
Canada's defence industry is not capable of survival without sharing U.S. research, development, design components and machine tools. Therefore it is time the present Government faced the reality that its leanings toward socialist friends while not protecting our own national security will result in severe limitations on Canada's historical participation in American military production, and no doubt could cause problems with the $3 billion Canadian offset package negotiated as part of Canada's $5 billion purchase of the McDonnell Douglas F-18, particularly if limits are placed on U.S. industrial offset agreements as per the monitoring Bill H.R. 2057 which is before Congress again this year.
